platforms.title: Sudden Hearing Loss vs. Earwax Buildup: How to Tell Them Apart
platforms.meta_description: Waking up with one ear suddenly muffled is easy to blame on earwax, but it can be sudden hearing loss. Why the first 72 hours matter for treatment.
platforms.body_html:
Ever woken up with one ear suddenly feeling muffled, like it's underwater? Most people assume it's earwax and wait it out for a few days, but that symptom can actually mean sudden sensorineural hearing loss. Unlike earwax buildup, this is a medical emergency where missing the treatment window can mean the hearing never fully comes back.

Why the treatment window matters so much

Sudden hearing loss is a sharp drop in hearing in one ear, over hours to a few days, with no obvious cause. The exact mechanism isn't fully understood, but it's thought to involve inflammation or blood flow problems inside the inner ear. What matters most is that starting steroid treatment quickly makes a real difference in the odds of recovering hearing. Getting treated within 72 hours of the symptom starting, ideally sooner, gives the best chance of it coming back.

Telling it apart from earwax buildup matters here. Earwax buildup usually develops gradually over days to weeks, often getting worse after a shower or swimming when the wax swells. Sudden hearing loss, on the other hand, arrives exactly as the name says — suddenly, usually within hours.

How to tell them apart, and how fast you need to act

First, you can point to roughly when it started, and it got noticeably worse within a day or two. Dizziness or ringing in the ear alongside it, without any pain, is also typical of sudden hearing loss.

Second, trying to clear it yourself with an ear pick or cotton swab doesn't change anything, or the muffled feeling gets worse. With true earwax buildup, hearing usually improves right after the wax is removed. With sudden hearing loss, nothing inside the ear canal changes the outcome.

If either of those signs shows up, see an ENT or go to the emergency room right away instead of waiting it out. Starting steroid treatment within that 72-hour window gives the best odds of hearing coming back. The longer treatment is delayed, the less effective it becomes, and after about a week recovery gets significantly harder.

An ENT confirms the diagnosis with a hearing test, comparing both ears to measure exactly how much hearing has dropped and at which frequencies. That test also rules out earwax and other obvious causes on the spot, which is part of why seeing a doctor beats waiting to see if it clears up on its own. Recovery outcomes vary a lot from person to person — some people regain hearing almost completely, others are left with some permanent loss even with prompt treatment, and a few don't recover much at all. That range is exactly why acting fast matters: starting treatment early gives the best odds, but it's never a guarantee, and none of that uncertainty changes if someone waits an extra week hoping it's just wax.

The takeaway: if one ear suddenly goes muffled, don't assume it's earwax — see a doctor before the treatment window closes. This article is for general health information; consult a medical professional for diagnosis and treatment.
